title: Training Methods
description: Explore the main training methods, what each develops, their advantages, and sporting examples for each.
content_html:
Why Do Different Athletes Train Differently?

Not every athlete trains the same way — a marathon runner, a sprinter and a gymnast all have very different physical demands. Each training method targets a specific component of fitness and is therefore suited to particular sports and performers. Knowing which method to use — and why — is a key skill for coaches and performers alike. This lesson covers the main methods of training and their advantages.

Continuous Training

Continuous training involves exercising at a constant, moderate intensity for a prolonged period — usually 20 minutes or more — without rest intervals. It is the most commonly associated method with cardiovascular endurance because it keeps the heart rate elevated steadily within the aerobic training zone. The advantages of continuous training include its simplicity (no specialist equipment needed), low cost, and the fact it can be done almost anywhere. It is particularly popular with distance runners, cyclists and swimmers. A marathon runner such as Eliud Kipchoge would use long, steady runs to develop their aerobic base and cardiovascular endurance.

Fartlek Training

The word "fartlek" comes from Swedish and means "speed play". Fartlek training combines steady-paced aerobic running with unplanned or planned bursts of faster effort, such as sprinting to a lamp post or accelerating uphill. It develops both cardiovascular endurance and speed endurance, making it ideal for games players who have to switch between different intensities. Advantages include variety (which reduces boredom), flexibility (the performer chooses when to sprint) and its ability to replicate the unpredictable demands of team sports. A football midfielder or rugby player benefits greatly from fartlek sessions because match play involves constant changes of pace.

Key Fact

Continuous training stays at a constant moderate pace; fartlek training mixes that steady pace with random bursts of higher intensity. Both methods develop cardiovascular endurance, but fartlek additionally improves speed endurance — making it more suitable for team-sport athletes.

Interval Training

Interval training involves alternating periods of high-intensity exercise with planned rest or low-intensity recovery periods. The work-to-rest ratio can be adjusted to target either the aerobic or anaerobic energy system depending on the intensity and duration of each interval. Shorter, more intense intervals (e.g. 30 seconds hard, 90 seconds rest) stress the anaerobic system, while longer intervals at a more moderate pace stress the aerobic system. The key advantage of interval training is its flexibility — coaches can precisely control the intensity, duration and number of repetitions to match the demands of the sport. A 400-metre runner might use 400 m repetitions with 3 minutes rest to develop their anaerobic threshold and speed endurance.

High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT)

High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is a specific form of interval training that uses very short bouts of near-maximal effort (typically 80–95% of maximum heart rate) separated by brief recovery periods. A common example is 20 seconds of all-out effort followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated 8 times (the Tabata protocol). HIIT primarily develops cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance simultaneously, and research shows it can achieve similar cardiovascular improvements to longer continuous sessions in a fraction of the time. Its main advantage is time efficiency. A footballer performing pre-season fitness work might use HIIT sprints to rapidly improve both aerobic capacity and anaerobic power.

Key Fact

HIIT is a specific, high-intensity variant of interval training. The key difference is that HIIT demands near-maximal effort during every work phase, making sessions much shorter but equally (or more) effective than longer aerobic workouts. Both HIIT and interval training can be adapted to improve aerobic or anaerobic components depending on the work-to-rest ratio used.

Circuit Training

Circuit training uses a series of exercise stations performed one after another, with minimal rest between stations. Each station targets a different muscle group or fitness component, so the body is kept working throughout. Circuits typically develop muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance at the same time, and can be adapted to include power or strength exercises. The advantages of circuit training include variety, the ability to train a large group simultaneously, and its adaptability — stations can be changed to suit any sport. A netball or basketball team might use circuit training in pre-season to build both aerobic fitness and muscular endurance across the whole body.

Weight / Resistance Training

Weight (or resistance) training involves working muscles against an external load — such as free weights, machines or body weight — through a controlled range of movement. The primary component developed depends on the sets and repetitions used: heavy loads with few repetitions (e.g. 3 sets of 5) develop muscular strength, while moderate loads with higher repetitions (e.g. 3 sets of 15–20) develop muscular endurance. Resistance training also contributes to power when explosive movements such as Olympic lifts are incorporated. An advantage is that it is highly specific — coaches can target exactly the muscle groups used in a sport. A shot putter or a rugby prop would use heavy resistance training to build maximal muscular strength.

The relationship between load and repetitions determines whether resistance training builds strength, power or endurance. A heavy load lifted for very few repetitions (1–5 reps) maximises muscular strength gains by recruiting the highest-threshold motor units. A moderate load lifted for 8–12 repetitions is optimal for muscular hypertrophy (size). A lighter load lifted for 15–20 or more repetitions trains muscular endurance, as the muscles must sustain repeated contractions over time. Explosive movements performed with moderate loads — such as a power clean — train power. Coaches should match the load-rep scheme to the athlete's position and the demands of their sport.

Plyometric Training

Plyometric training uses rapid stretching of a muscle followed immediately by an explosive contraction — a mechanism known as the stretch-shortening cycle. Examples include box jumps, bounding, depth jumps and clap press-ups. Plyometrics primarily develop power, which is the combination of strength and speed. They are particularly suited to athletes who need explosive movements — a high jumper, a basketball player or a volleyball player all require powerful jumps. An advantage is that plyometrics closely replicate the explosive demands of many sports, making them highly sport-specific. The main limitation is the high impact involved, so performers need a solid strength base before beginning plyometric training.

Flexibility Training

Flexibility training aims to improve the range of motion at joints. There are two main types specified. Static stretching involves holding a muscle in a lengthened position for typically 15–30 seconds; it is safe, easy to perform and effective at improving general flexibility. It is widely used in cool-downs and by gymnasts and dancers for whom a high range of movement is a core performance requirement. PNF stretching (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation) is a more advanced technique that involves contracting the target muscle isometrically while it is stretched, then relaxing and deepening the stretch. PNF typically produces greater flexibility gains than static stretching and is often used by physiotherapists and elite athletes. A gymnast or a dancer would use both methods regularly to maintain and improve their flexibility.

PNF stretching exploits the nervous system to achieve a greater range of motion. The technique typically follows three phases: first, the muscle is passively stretched to its limit; second, the athlete isometrically contracts the stretched muscle for around 5–10 seconds (pushing against a partner's or immovable resistance), which temporarily fatigues the motor neurones; third, the muscle is relaxed and the partner deepens the stretch further, taking advantage of the brief window when the muscle's stretch reflex is suppressed. This "post-contraction inhibition" allows the muscle to lengthen further than a static stretch alone would achieve. PNF requires a trained partner and is more time-consuming, which is why it tends to be used in high-performance settings rather than in general warm-ups.
exam_tip_html: Exam questions on training methods often ask you to identify the method, state the fitness component it develops, and give a sporting example — all three parts are usually needed for full marks. The most common mistakes are: confusing interval training with HIIT (HIIT is a specific, near-maximal version); saying continuous training develops muscular strength (it does not — it develops cardiovascular endurance); and forgetting to name both types of flexibility training (static and PNF). When the question asks you to "justify" a training method for an athlete, link the method's primary component to a specific demand of the sport.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Continuous training: steady pace, no rest — develops cardiovascular endurance. Best for distance runners and cyclists.
  • Fartlek training: varied pace with random bursts — develops cardiovascular endurance and speed endurance. Best for team-sport players.
  • Interval training: work then rest periods — can target aerobic or anaerobic fitness depending on the work-to-rest ratio. HIIT is a near-maximal, time-efficient variant.
  • Circuit training: multiple stations with little rest — develops muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance. Adaptable for team training.
  • Weight/resistance training: works muscles against load — develops muscular strength (heavy load, low reps) or muscular endurance (lighter load, high reps). Best for strength athletes.
  • Plyometric training: stretch-shortening cycle — develops power. Best for jumpers and explosive athletes. Requires a strength base.
  • Flexibility training: static (hold 15–30 s) and PNF (contract then deepen the stretch) — both develop flexibility. PNF produces greater gains.

practice_questions.text:
Which training method involves exercising at a constant, moderate pace for an extended period without rest?
A) Interval training
B) Fartlek training
C) Continuous training
D) Circuit training
State two advantages of fartlek training for a football player.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: it develops both aerobic and anaerobic fitness / it replicates the unpredictable intensity changes of match play / it is varied and reduces boredom / it is flexible as the performer decides when to increase pace / it can be performed on any terrain without specialist equipment. Answers must be distinct. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the work-to-rest ratio in interval training can be adapted to target different energy systems.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "shorter rest targets the anaerobic system"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "a short work period with long rest — such as 20 seconds effort, 2 minutes rest — stresses the anaerobic ATP-PC system, developing explosive speed"). A further developed or second mechanism scores 3 marks (e.g. add "longer, moderate-intensity intervals with shorter rest, such as 3 minutes work with 1 minute rest, keep heart rate elevated in the aerobic zone and develop cardiovascular endurance"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between static stretching and PNF stretching, and explain why PNF can produce greater flexibility gains.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): static stretching involves holding a muscle at its end range for 15–30 seconds without movement (1 mark); PNF involves contracting the stretched muscle isometrically then relaxing and deepening the stretch with the help of a partner (1 mark). Explanation of PNF advantage (up to 2 marks): the isometric contraction temporarily fatigues the motor neurones (1 mark), which suppresses the stretch reflex and allows the muscle to lengthen further in the relaxation phase, achieving a greater range of motion than static stretching alone (1 mark for developed mechanism). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A strength and conditioning coach is designing a 6-week pre-season programme for a basketball team. The coach wants to improve both explosive jumping power and cardiovascular fitness.

Discuss which two training methods the coach should select and justify each choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two clearly identified methods (e.g. plyometric training and HIIT/interval training) with developed justification linked to basketball demands. Plyometrics: develops power through the stretch-shortening cycle; box jumps and depth jumps directly replicate the explosive jumping required for rebounds and shot-blocking (2 marks for developed justification). HIIT or interval training: develops cardiovascular fitness time-efficiently; short sprint intervals replicate the high-intensity bursts of basketball where players sprint, stop and sprint repeatedly throughout a 40-minute game (2 marks for developed justification). A comment on how the two methods complement each other scores the final mark.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two methods identified, justified with some reference to basketball.
Developing (2 marks): One method identified with some justification.
Emerging (1 mark): A relevant method named without justification. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A long-distance cyclist wants to improve their cardiovascular endurance over a 16-week training block. They currently only use continuous training.

Evaluate the extent to which adding HIIT sessions would improve their performance more than continuing with continuous training alone.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing both sides. For HIIT: research suggests HIIT can produce equivalent or superior cardiovascular adaptations in less time; the high intensity stresses both aerobic and anaerobic systems, improving lactate threshold and VO2 max more rapidly; variety reduces boredom and psychological fatigue from long sessions. Against / limitations of HIIT: continuous training builds the aerobic base essential for event-specific endurance; HIIT sessions are very demanding and recovery must be managed to avoid overtraining; a cyclist who races for 3+ hours needs sustained moderate-intensity endurance that HIIT alone cannot fully replicate. Substantiated judgement: a combined approach (periodised mix of continuous and HIIT) is most effective — HIIT for adaptations, continuous training for race-specific endurance.
Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides addressed with some evidence/reasoning; some attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points largely one-sided or limited development.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which training method primarily develops power by using the stretch-shortening cycle?
Which component of fitness does continuous training most directly develop?
In weight training, using a heavy load with a low number of repetitions primarily develops _____.
PNF stretching involves isometrically _____ the stretched muscle before relaxing and deepening the stretch, which suppresses the stretch reflex and allows a greater range of motion.
Match each training method to the fitness component it primarily develops.
right: Power — through rapid stretch-shortening cycle movements such as box jumps
Muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance — multiple stations targeting different muscle groups
Cardiovascular endurance and speed endurance — varied-pace running with bursts of higher intensity

flashcard_questions.a: Steady-pace exercise for 20+ minutes without rest, developing cardiovascular endurance.

flashcard_questions.q: Which extra fitness component does fartlek develop beyond cardiovascular endurance?
flashcard_questions.a: Speed endurance, from bursts of higher-intensity effort within the session.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the work-to-rest ratio in interval training determine?
flashcard_questions.a: Whether the aerobic or anaerobic energy system is primarily stressed.

flashcard_questions.q: How does HIIT differ from standard interval training?
flashcard_questions.a: HIIT requires near-maximal effort each interval, so sessions are very short.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of athlete benefits most from circuit training?
flashcard_questions.a: Team-sport players needing both muscular endurance and cardiovascular fitness.

flashcard_questions.q: How many reps are used in resistance training for muscular strength?
flashcard_questions.a: Typically 1 to 5 repetitions with a heavy load.

flashcard_questions.q: What physical mechanism does plyometric training use to develop power?
flashcard_questions.a: The stretch-shortening cycle: rapid muscle stretch then explosive contraction.

flashcard_questions.q: Which sport performers would most benefit from plyometric training?
flashcard_questions.a: Athletes who need explosive jumping power in their sport.
Holding a muscle at its end range for 15 to 30 seconds.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does PNF stretching produce greater gains than static stretching?
flashcard_questions.a: Isometric contraction suppresses the stretch reflex, allowing deeper muscle lengthening.

flashcard_questions.q: What fitness component does resistance training with 15 to 20 repetitions develop?
What makes HIIT attractive to time-limited athletes?
flashcard_questions.a: It achieves similar cardiovascular gains to longer sessions in far less time.

glossary_terms.definition: A structured approach to physical exercise designed to improve a specific component of fitness through particular types of work and rest.
Training performed at a constant, steady pace for an extended period without rest, typically lasting 20 minutes or more at moderate intensity.
A training method that mixes continuous exercise with random or structured bursts of higher-intensity effort, developing both aerobic and anaerobic fitness.
Training that aims to increase the range of motion at a joint by lengthening the muscles and connective tissue surrounding it.
A training method using explosive movements that exploit the stretch-shortening cycle to develop muscular power.
